A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MENLO framework, dataset, and experiments. Their main texts, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching retained material across appendix renumbering.

before.justification: V2 reports original annotation results, multilingual judge evaluations, SFT/RL experiments, reward ablations, and human evaluation of post-trained responses in Sections 2–5 and the appendices.

after.justification: V3 retains these original empirical results and additionally reports judge-output examples, an output-length finding, and bootstrap statistical analyses in Appendices F–G.

M1.justification: The grading procedures, SFT objectives, GRPO training, composite reward formula, and use of pairwise judges as generative reward models are unchanged. New annotation documentation and output examples do not establish changes to the method.

E1.justification: Both versions use MENLO’s 47 language varieties and four quality dimensions, with the same three-dimension policy-training scope and ten-language human evaluation. BiGGen Bench is added only to the descriptive dataset comparison; it is not evaluated.

E2.justification: The eight benchmarked judge models, SFT/RL comparisons, reward ablation variants, and policy-evaluation judges are retained. Appendices F–G examine existing models and comparisons without adding a new evaluated comparator.

E3.justification: The existing split description, metrics, model configurations, training budgets, and human-evaluation procedures are retained. V3’s new Table 2 note lists 1,776 test examples, but does not resolve the pre-existing inconsistency between 1,766 pairs and 3,552 responses in Section 3 or establish a revised split. The new bootstrap procedure is assessed under E5.

E4.justification: Appendix F adds qualitative comparisons of pairwise judge outputs with and without rubrics for gpt-4.1, Llama4-Scout, and Qwen3-32B. These extend the existing rubric analysis with inspectable reasoning and grades; the reward, multitask, and cross-language ablations remain unchanged.

E5.justification: New Appendix G introduces 5,000 bootstrap resamples, 95% confidence intervals, and significance reporting for RL versus SFT, pairwise versus pointwise evaluation, and rubric effects. This substantially expands statistical reporting beyond v2’s point estimates and agreement measures. It does not establish additional independent training runs.

E6.justification: Existing benchmark tables retain their numerical results. Appendices F–G add example grades, the finding that rubrics produce 15–20% longer judge outputs, and statistical effect estimates and significance outcomes. Some new estimates do not reconcile with retained tables, so they cannot be treated as established performance improvements over v2.

T1.justification: The composite reward equation and existing mathematical content are unchanged. V3 adds no theorem, proof, formal assumption, or substantive derivation; the bootstrap analysis is empirical statistical reporting.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction’s contribution list, and conclusion retain the same claims about MENLO, pairwise judging, multitask RL with reward shaping, and generative reward modeling. The qualification that automated judges overestimate improvements relative to humans is also retained.

C2.justification: Appendix A.1 newly acknowledges that independently authored prompts would better capture native discourse structures than localized English templates, explaining the resource tradeoff. Appendix F also attributes longer judge outputs to explicit references to grading criteria. Existing limitations concerning localized factuality and human–judge discrepancies remain.

D1.justification: New Appendix B substantially expands annotation reproducibility information: vendor and expert staffing, language certification, 30-minute interviews, an 80% qualification threshold, retraining, feedback schedules, and quality-assurance procedures. These document the existing annotation process rather than establish changed collection practices. Model-training details and dataset access remain unchanged.

R1.justification: V3 adds BiGGen Bench (Kim et al., 2025) to Table 2 and the references, modestly broadening comparison with prior datasets. Other reference changes mainly update publication metadata for already cited works; the central research positioning is retained.

P1.justification: V3 modestly compresses and edits the main narrative, adds Appendices B, F, and G, and renumbers the retained appendices. It also introduces a reproducibility statement, relocates the compensation disclosure into an ethics statement, and updates the publication header. The main section sequence and argument remain substantially intact.

P2.justification: Table 2 gains a BiGGen Bench row and a dataset-size note. V3 adds six judge-output figures, Figures 18–23, with blue highlighting of rubric references, enlarges several appendix displays including Tables 13, 22, and 23, and relocates some retained tables. Existing scientific figures and benchmark table structures are otherwise preserved.

improvement.justification: The annotation documentation, explicit localization limitation, and judge-output examples improve transparency. However, new Appendix G reports a 7.56-point Qwen3-4B pairwise Macro-F1 gain versus 12.40 points in retained Table 3 without explaining the difference. Its gpt-4.1 rubric-gain confidence interval of 3.7–7.3 points also excludes Table 4’s 9.97-point gain. These unresolved discrepancies weaken the added statistical support, preventing a reliable net quality judgment.
